Mickey Munday sits down with VladTV to reflect on his early life in South Florida before the Cocaine Cowboys era. Born in Miami in 1945, Munday explains how the city functioned as a major World War II military hub, with Navy and Army Air Corps sites later becoming places like Miami Dade College, FIU, Opa-locka, and Key Biscayne. He describes a seasonal, pre-air-conditioning Miami shaped by limestone mining, canals, swamps, construction, and postwar growth.

Munday also shares memories of boating as a kid, his father’s concrete block business, trips through South Florida, Cape Canaveral, the Florida Keys, and Disney World before it opened. The interview then follows his path from high school track athlete and motorcycle builder to taking over the family company during the 1970s recession, before the events that led him into drug transportation and the world later documented in Cocaine Cowboys.

--------
Rainwater sits down with DJ Vlad to clarify the chaotic days after Dallas rapper Mo3 was killed, including what really happened when Boosie Badazz was shot in Dallas just three days later. He corrects details about the incident, saying the vehicle hit was one of his driver’s trucks in an alley, not the version often repeated online, and places the scene around Big T Plaza as Boosie was in town for a show and to pick up jewelry.

Rainwater also pushes back on rumors that Boosie came to Dallas looking for revenge after his joint work with Mo3, including the Badazz Mo3 project. He says a fake Boosie page fueled tensions with posts aimed at Dallas, while the city was already on edge, with more than 30 shootings that weekend. The conversation covers Oak Cliff, Big T, online misinformation, and the tense aftermath of Mo3’s death.

In this VladTV interview, Joby Walters reflects on becoming a Hells Angel and the motorcycle club politics that shaped Arizona and California. Walters discusses the Dirty Dozen’s influence in Arizona, the Hells Angels’ expansion through Yuma, and tensions involving the Mongols, Vagos, Bandidos and Outlaws over territory and the California bottom rocker. He also addresses the lead-up to the River Run riot, explaining his view that the Hells Angels were not a criminal organization as a whole, while acknowledging that individual members broke the law. Walters opens up about staying away from drug use during his years in the club, the impact of meth on bikers around him, and moments in Durango and San Bernardino that reinforced his sobriety. A candid look at outlaw biker culture, club loyalty, law enforcement scrutiny, and life inside a notorious motorcycle world.

In this VladTV interview, John Franzese Jr. reflects on the complicated legacy of his father, John Franzese Sr., who died in 2020 at age 103. Speaking with Vlad, Franzese Jr. addresses long-running rumors that his father was linked to dozens of killings, including stories tied to Coney Island and alleged work connected to the Genovese and Profaci crime families. He also discusses the code of silence, being labeled a “rat,” and the moral questions surrounding cooperation, responsibility, and mob violence.

Franzese Jr. explains why he chose not to attend his father’s funeral, saying he did not want his presence, U.S. Marshals security, or family tensions to shift attention away from the service. He also notes that Michael Franzese did not attend. A candid look at organized crime, family loyalty, and the aftermath of life inside the mob.

Jimmy DiModica sits down with Vlad for a candid look at life after prison, family loyalty, and the changing face of organized crime. He reflects on his father’s release in his 80s, his mother’s unwavering devotion, and how he supported himself after leaving the Mafia world behind. DiModica also explains why he believes the mob still exists in 2026, adapting into areas like cyber crime and the stock market wherever greed creates opportunity.

The conversation turns to cooperation in mob cases, with Vlad comparing DiModica’s stance to figures like Sammy “The Bull” Gravano, Michael Franzese, John Junior, and Norby Walters. DiModica emphasizes that he never cooperated with authorities, calling himself a rarity among former mob figures interviewed on the platform. He also teases documented stories involving Elvis Presley’s stepmother, talk shows, and a possible book.
